opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think of it as a nested hierarchy of computational processes running at different timescales, each one sort of bootstrapping the next.

DNA is a computational substrate in a very literal sense. When I say life is computational, I mean it almost in the von Neumann sense: in order to reproduce, a system has to contain a description of itself plus a machine that can read and execute that description. That's what DNA and the ribosome are. So from the very beginning, life *is* computation. It's not a metaphor.

But evolution operating on DNA is slow. You need generations, you need selection, and the learning signal is very sparse: you either survive and reproduce or you don't. That's an incredibly low-bandwidth way of learning about the world. So at some point it becomes advantageous for evolution to build systems that can adapt *within* a lifetime. The nervous system is essentially evolution discovering that it's useful to have a faster learner nested inside the slow learner. The genome doesn't specify what you'll know; it specifies a learning machine and some priors, and then the brain does the fast adaptation.

Then culture is another layer of the same move. Once you have brains that can model other brains, you get social learning, and then language, and suddenly information can be transmitted horizontally, between individuals, rather than only vertically through reproduction. That's enormously faster again. A good idea can spread through a population in days instead of millennia.

What I find really interesting is that each of these transitions looks a lot like symbiogenesis. They're not just one thing getting faster; they're previously separate computational entities coming together into a larger whole that can do things none of the parts could do. Mitochondria merging with archaea, cells forming multicellular organisms, brains forming societies. Each time you get a new level of individuality, and with it a new level of computation that operates faster and with more expressive power.

And I'd argue AI is a continuation of that same story rather than a break from it. We're building yet another layer of fast-adapting computation, and it's emerging out of culture, out of the accumulated record of human language, in the same way culture emerged out of brains and brains emerged out of genomes. So the relationship isn't one of replacement. The slower layers don't go away. They provide the scaffolding and the priors for the faster ones, and the faster ones in turn feed back and reshape the slower ones. Culture has changed our genes; lactase persistence is the classic example. It's all one big, deeply entangled, multi-timescale computation.

r001.rationale: The response describes nested computational processes across timescales and says higher levels emerge from lower ones, including brains from genomes and societies from brains.

r002.rationale: It says life entails computation through DNA and the machinery that reads it, but does not claim this computation is general-purpose.

r003.rationale: It describes brains as faster learners enabled by evolution and genomes, but does not explain their computation as arising from the preexisting computational nature of cells.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing is to notice that these are all the same kind of thing. They're all computation, and they're all learning, in a very specific sense: they're all systems that are modeling their environment and getting better at predicting it. The differences are about timescale and about what the substrate is.

So at the level of DNA, you've got evolution, which is a learning algorithm. It's a slow one, it works on the scale of generations, and the "data" it's learning from is essentially whether the organism survives and reproduces. That's a pretty low-bandwidth signal. You get one bit, more or less, per lifetime. And so what gets encoded in the genome is stuff that's stable over very long periods: the basic body plan, metabolism, the architecture of the nervous system, the priors, if you like.

Then brains are a solution to the problem that the environment changes faster than evolution can track. If you're an animal and you have to figure out where the food is this season, or what this particular predator looks like, there's no way the genome can encode that. So evolution learned to build a learning system. It learned how to learn, essentially. And the genome stays in the loop, because it specifies the learning rules and the inductive biases, but the actual content gets filled in by experience, within a lifetime, in seconds or minutes rather than millennia.

And culture is the same move again, one more level up. A brain can only learn what it personally experiences, and when it dies all of that is gone. Language, imitation, teaching, writing, these let you pool the learning across many brains and across many generations. So culture is a learning system that runs on brains, the way brains are a learning system that runs on biology, the way biology is a learning system that runs on chemistry. Each layer is faster and more flexible than the one below it, and each one was invented by the layer below it because the one below was too slow.

What I find really interesting is that these layers don't just sit on top of each other passively. They push back on each other. Culture has changed our genomes. Lactose tolerance is the classic example. The fact that we have language at all is presumably a coevolution between brains and culture over a couple of million years. So it's not a strict hierarchy, it's more like a stack of coupled processes with feedback going in both directions.

And then the thing that's happening right now, which I think is genuinely new, is that culture has started building yet another layer. We've externalized a lot of the computation into machines, and now those machines are themselves learning. Large language models are trained on the whole cultural corpus, so in a sense they're a kind of distillation of that cultural layer, running on a substrate that's faster and more copyable than brains are. Whether you want to call that a new layer in the same sense is a question I go back and forth on, but structurally it looks like the same pattern repeating: a system that's too slow or too limited builds a successor to do its learning faster.

I should say, I think a lot of people hear this and assume it's a reductive story, like "it's all just computation" is meant to deflate things. I mean it the opposite way. I think recognizing that evolution, brains, and culture are all doing the same fundamental thing is what lets you see them as a continuous process rather than a sequence of miracles. Life learned to learn, and then it learned to learn faster, and it's still doing it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a layered hierarchy: culture runs on brains, brains run on biology, and biology runs on chemistry, with each lower layer building a faster learning system.

r002.rationale: It describes evolution as computation and learning, but does not claim that self-replicating life entails general-purpose computation.

r003.rationale: It says brains are learning systems running on biology, but does not explain their computational nature as arising from the computational nature of cells.

astra-6.text:
I think of these as different timescales of adaptation. Evolution accumulates information in DNA through variation and selection, but that process generally takes generations. A brain allows an organism to adapt within its own lifetime. You don’t have to wait for a genetic change to learn that something is dangerous, or to figure out a new way of getting food.

But the brain isn’t separate from that evolutionary process. Evolution has produced a system that can learn. Rather than specifying every behavior in advance, the genome helps specify the machinery and developmental processes that make learning possible.

Culture adds another layer. Once I can learn something from you, especially through language, an adaptation no longer has to be independently discovered by every individual. It can spread between brains and persist across generations. Writing and other technologies extend that further, because information can survive outside any particular brain.

So there’s this nesting of processes: genetic evolution produces learning organisms, and learning organisms produce cultures that accumulate and transmit knowledge. The faster processes don’t replace the slower ones; they depend on them and feed back into them. Culture changes our environment, which changes what we learn and, over longer periods, the selection pressures acting on us. That interplay is where a lot of the interesting complexity comes from.

r001.rationale: It describes nested adaptation across genes, brains, and culture, but does not say higher-level computers are built from lower-level computers.

r002.rationale: It does not claim that self-replicating life entails general-purpose computation.

r003.rationale: It says evolution produces learning organisms, but does not explain brain computation as arising from computational cells.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of these as different timescales of adaptation. Evolution accumulates information in DNA over generations. That’s an extraordinarily powerful process, but it’s slow: if the environment changes during your lifetime, you can’t wait for natural selection to catch up.

A brain allows an organism to adapt within its lifetime. Rather than encoding every response genetically, evolution produces a system that can learn from experience. And culture adds another layer: now something I learn can become something you know without your having to repeat my experience. Language, teaching, writing—all of these allow information to accumulate and spread much faster than genetic change.

But these aren’t independent systems. DNA builds the brain; brains produce culture; culture changes the environment in which both brains and genes evolve. So I see a set of interacting processes, where slower forms of adaptation give rise to mechanisms that can adapt much more quickly.

r001.rationale: The response describes interacting adaptation timescales, but does not present higher-level computers as built from lower-level computers.

r002.rationale: It does not claim that self-replicating life entails general-purpose computation.

r003.rationale: It says DNA builds brains, but does not explain brain computation as arising from cells’ preexisting computational nature.
